title: Verbal-logical thinking and reading skills: A cross-lag analysis of mutual influence at the stage “kindergarten—primary school”
abstract: Context and relevance. The relevance of a longitudinal analysis of cause-and-effect relationships between verbal-logical thinking and the acquisition of reading skills stems from the need to address a fundamental problem in psychology—the relationship between mental development and learning. In practical psychology, this research is associated with the search for early individual psychological markers of potential learning difficulties. The processes of mental development and learning to read are closely interrelated throughout general education, but the direction and strength of these causal relationships may change during the transition from preschool to the initial stage of general education. Objective. This study examines the interplay between verbal-logical thinking and reading skills during the transition from kindergarten to the first grade of primary school. Methods and materials. A total of 260 children (50,1% female) participated in the study at two time points: during their preschool preparatory groups (Mage = 6,82, SD = 0,3) and one year later, following the completion of their first year of primary education (Mage = 7,83, SD = 0,3). Verbal-logical thinking was assessed using a mental development test measuring abstraction, classification and generalization, and analogical reasoning. Reading proficiency was evaluated according to reading method, ranging from non-reading to reading in whole words. Data were analyzed using cross-lagged panel structural equation modeling. Results. The analysis of cross-lagged relationships revealed a bidirectional nature of the relationship between verbal-logical thinking and reading proficiency during the transition from preschool to primary school. The most pronounced direct proportional effect was observed in the direction where the level of reading proficiency achieved by the end of the preschool period influences the subsequent development of cognitive operations—abstraction, classification and generalization, and analogical reasoning—at the onset of formal schooling. Conclusions. The specific nature of the causal relationship between the development of verbal-logical thinking and reading acquisition was identified and interpreted within the framework of cultural-historical psychology.
